output.title: The middle is the part that matters
output.body:
The quiet cost of before-and-after framing is that it makes a workflow look cleaner than it is. A small business owner sees “before manual invoicing, after automation” and gets asked to trust the gap without checking the middle: setup time, learning, integration friction, and the handoff from demo to daily use. That middle is where the real decision lives.

For a bounded Bareni decision, I would not start with “Will AI do it?” I would start with one recurring workflow and ask whether it is repeatable enough to test. That is what the free 30-minute diagnostic is for: identify the one recurring workflow, say honestly whether AI fits, and, if it does, define pilot scope, fixed price, and measures. Timings are intended scopes, not guarantees.

A practical next step for the owner is simple: write down one process you repeat every week and the measure you would accept before you commit. Not a vague improvement, but the actual threshold. If you cannot name that in plain English, the “after” is still a story, not a decision.

The real before-and-after test happens inside your workflow, not in a vendor demo.
